source.title: Indian Polity (question set written from its topics)

chapter.name: Concept of the Constitution
chapter.blurb: The meaning, functions, qualities and classification of constitutions, and constitutionalism.

scope_in.item: Definitions, functions, qualities, classification and constitutionalism in depth

concepts.name: The definitions of a constitution, matched to their authors
concepts.description: Gilchrist, Gettell, Wheare, and Wade and Phillips and their key phrases.
concepts.idea: Each scholar defines the constitution with a distinct emphasis on rules, principles, system or legal sanctity.
concepts.rule: Gilchrist: the body of rules or laws which determine the organisation of government, the distribution of powers to the various organs of government, and the general principles on which these powers are exercised. Gettell: the fundamental principles that determine the form of a state, including how it is organised, the distribution of sovereign powers among the organs of government, the scope and manner of exercise of governmental functions and the relation of the government to the people. Wheare: the whole system of government of a country, the collection of rules which establish and regulate or govern the government. Wade and Phillips: a document having a special legal sanctity which sets out the framework and principal functions of the organs of government of a State and declares the principles governing their operation.
concepts.example: Wheare speaks of 'the whole system of government of a country'.

o: The principles governing the operation of the organs of government

questions.q: Which feature of a constitution do Wade and Phillips stress that others do not?

o: Special legal sanctity as a document

questions.q: 'The collection of rules which establish and regulate or govern the government' is from
questions.a: Wheare

questions.q: 'General principles on which these powers are exercised' is from
questions.a: Gilchrist

questions.q: Match Gilchrist and Wade and Phillips with their key idea.
questions.a: Gilchrist stresses rules determining organisation and distribution of powers, while Wade and Phillips stress a document with special legal sanctity framing the organs of government.

questions.q: What three aspects of government does Gettell's definition cover besides the form of the state?
questions.a: The way the state is organised, distribution of sovereign powers, and scope and manner of exercising functions, with relation to the people.

questions.q: Which two authors mention 'distribution of powers'?
questions.a: Gilchrist and Gettell

questions.q: Show how all four definitions share the idea that a constitution regulates government.
questions.a: Each speaks of rules, principles or a system governing the organisation and functioning of government, though with different emphasis.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.a: Wheare - system of rules; Gilchrist - organisation and distribution of powers
o: Wheare - system of rules; Gilchrist - organisation and distribution of powers
Wheare - legal sanctity; Wade - system of rules
Gettell - document; Gilchrist - form of state

questions.q: Compare Wheare's and Wade and Phillips' definitions.
questions.a: Wheare sees the whole system of rules that regulate government, while Wade and Phillips stress a special legal document that frames the organs and declares principles of operation.

questions.q: Why do definitions of a constitution differ although the concept is the same?
questions.a: Each scholar looks at a different aspect, such as legal force, distribution of power, form of state or the whole system, so the definitions overlap but stress different elements.

questions.q: Which of the four definitions best fits India's Constitution? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned choice is accepted, for example Wade and Phillips since India has a document with legal sanctity.

questions.q: Make a table of four authors with the key words of their definitions.
questions.a: A table with Gilchrist, Gettell, Wheare and Wade and Phillips and correct key words.

concepts.name: The eight functions of a constitution, one by one
concepts.description: Each of Bulmer's eight functions explained separately with examples.
concepts.idea: Each function of a constitution answers a specific need of a political community.
concepts.rule: (1) Declare and define the boundaries of the political community. (2) Declare and define the nature and authority of the political community, for example that sovereignty rests with the people. (3) Express the identity and values of a national community, as in a Preamble. (4) Declare and define the rights and duties of citizens. (5) Establish and regulate political institutions such as legislature, executive and judiciary. (6) Divide or share power between different layers of government or sub-state communities, as in a federation. (7) Declare the official religious identity of the state and the relationship between sacred and secular authority, as in a secular or theocratic state. (8) Commit states to particular social, economic or developmental goals, as in Directive Principles.
concepts.example: Directive Principles commit the Indian State to social and economic goals.

questions.a: Declaring the religious identity of the state

o: Defining the political community and its territory

questions.q: Give the function performed by Articles 25 to 28 and by Article 51A.
questions.a: Articles 25 to 28 relate to religion and the State (function 7 and rights), and Article 51A declares citizens' duties.

questions.q: Identify the functions served by a federal constitution with a Bill of Rights.
questions.a: It divides power between layers of government and declares the rights of citizens.

questions.q: Which function is served by creating a Supreme Court?

questions.q: Explain how all eight functions can be seen in the Indian Constitution with one example each for four functions.
questions.a: Article 1 defines boundaries, the Preamble expresses identity and values, Part III declares rights, and the Directive Principles commit the State to goals.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.a: Sharing power - federal division; Identity - Preamble
o: Sharing power - federal division; Identity - Preamble

questions.q: Compare defining boundaries and dividing power in function.
questions.a: Defining boundaries says who and what territory the community includes, while dividing power distributes authority among layers of government or communities.

questions.q: Why can a constitution's function of setting goals cause debate?
questions.a: Goals like social justice may bind future governments to policy directions, so some see them as guidance and others as restrictions on democratic choice.

questions.q: Which two functions are most essential for a new democracy? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned choice is accepted, such as establishing institutions and declaring rights.

questions.a: A table listing the eight functions with correct Indian examples.

concepts.name: Qualities of a good constitution in application
concepts.description: Applying brevity, clarity, definiteness, comprehensiveness, suitability, stability and adaptability to cases.
concepts.idea: The seven qualities can be used to judge how good a constitution is in particular situations.
concepts.rule: Brevity avoids unwanted provisions; a lengthy constitution with too many details creates confusion in interpretation. Clarity requires clear terms since complicated language reduces understanding. Definiteness means fixed meaning, because ambiguity increases the discretion of judges. Comprehensiveness means laying down powers of government and the rights and duties of citizens fully to reduce controversy and litigation. Suitability means reflecting the people's needs and their historical, socio-cultural, economic and political conditions. Stability means facilitating political stability and not allowing easy tampering, which strengthens obedience. Adaptability means being dynamic, able to adjust to changing situations, a living document.
concepts.example: A constitution that cannot be changed at all lacks adaptability.

questions.a: tampering

questions.a: The constitution must fit the people's historical and social conditions
o: The constitution must fit the people's historical and social conditions

questions.a: Stability

questions.q: Which quality is threatened when a constitution can never be amended?
questions.a: Adaptability

questions.q: A constitution using very complicated legal language lacks
questions.a: clarity

questions.q: A constitution missing any provision on citizens' rights lacks
questions.a: comprehensiveness

questions.q: A country adopts another nation's constitution word for word. Which quality may be weak and why?
questions.a: Suitability, because it may not reflect its own history, culture and conditions.

questions.q: A single Article has two possible meanings and courts disagree. Which quality is missing and what follows?
questions.a: Definiteness is missing, and judges gain discretion in interpretation, causing disputes.

questions.q: Which two qualities may need balancing against each other?
questions.a: Brevity and comprehensiveness

questions.q: Evaluate the Indian Constitution against brevity and comprehensiveness.
questions.a: It is very lengthy and detailed, so weak on brevity, but it covers powers, rights and duties comprehensively, reducing gaps.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.a: Stability - resists easy tampering; Adaptability - changes with needs
o: Stability - resists easy tampering; Adaptability - changes with needs
Stability - changes with needs; Adaptability - resists tampering

questions.q: Compare stability and adaptability.
questions.a: Stability keeps the constitution from being easily changed, while adaptability lets it change with new needs; a good constitution balances both.

questions.q: Why does definiteness matter for the independence of the judiciary?
questions.a: Ambiguity gives judges wide discretion in interpretation, which may make decisions unpredictable, so clear meaning limits that discretion.

questions.q: Which quality would you rank first? Give one reason.
questions.a: A reasoned choice is accepted.

questions.q: Create seven scenarios, one for each quality, showing a constitution that lacks it.
questions.a: Seven short scenarios, each matching a quality.

concepts.name: Types of constitution and country examples
concepts.description: A matrix of countries by evolved or enacted, written or unwritten, rigid or flexible, federal or unitary.
concepts.idea: Each country can be placed in several categories at once.
concepts.rule: Evolved (cumulative): British. Enacted (conventional): American and Indian. Written (documentary, codified): USA, Canada, Japan, France, India. Unwritten (non-documentary, uncodified): UK, New Zealand, Israel. Flexible (elastic): UK, New Zealand. Rigid (inelastic): USA, Australia, Switzerland. India is neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis. Federal: USA, Switzerland, Australia, Canada, Russia, Brazil. Unitary: UK, France, Japan, China, Italy, Norway. India has both federal and unitary provisions, so is quasi-federal (Wheare). By Bulmer's archetypes, a procedural constitution defines legal and political structures and limits, and a prescriptive constitution assumes or imposes a broad consensus on societal goals.
concepts.example: The UK is an evolved, unwritten, flexible and unitary constitution.

questions.q: Why can a written constitution be flexible or rigid?

concepts.name: Rigid and flexible, and procedural and prescriptive: scholars and terms
concepts.description: Bryce, Wheare and Bulmer and the alternative names for each type.
concepts.idea: Bryce classified rigid and flexible constitutions; Bulmer described procedural and prescriptive ones.
concepts.rule: Lord James Bryce gave the classification into rigid and flexible. A rigid constitution cannot be amended like ordinary law and needs a special procedure; it separates constitutional law from ordinary law; it is also called an inelastic constitution. A flexible constitution can be amended in the same way as ordinary laws and does not distinguish constitutional and ordinary law; it is also called an elastic constitution. K.C. Wheare called the Indian Constitution quasi-federal. Elliot Bulmer identified two archetypes: procedural, which sets out structures of public institutions and legal limits of government power to protect democratic processes and fundamental human rights; and prescriptive, which in addition assumes or attempts to impose a broad consensus on common societal goals that public authorities must strive to achieve. The difference relates to the nature and purposes of the document itself.
concepts.example: A flexible constitution is also called an elastic constitution.

concepts.name: Constitutionalism: scholars and Henkin's eight elements one by one
concepts.description: Definitions by Friedrich, Roucek, Wheare and Ybema, and each element of constitutionalism.
concepts.idea: Each of the eight elements limits government power in a specific way.
concepts.rule: Friedrich: constitutionalism is a system of effective restraints upon governmental action, a body of rules ensuring fair play and making government responsible. Roucek: essentially limited government, the antithesis of government by the unrestrained will of rulers. Wheare: constitutional government means government according to rule as opposed to arbitrary government, limited by the constitution and not only by the desires and capacities of those who exercise power. Ybema: government is constitutional only when rulers are subject to a body of rules and principles limiting their power. Louis Henkin's eight elements: popular sovereignty; rule of law; democratic (responsible and accountable) government; separation of powers (checks and balances); independent judiciary; civilian control of the military; police governed by law and judicial control; respect for individual rights. Unlimited power jeopardises freedom, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
concepts.example: Henkin listed eight elements of constitutionalism.

questions.q: Match Friedrich and Roucek with their definitions.
questions.a: Friedrich: a system of effective restraints on governmental action; Roucek: limited government, the antithesis of the unrestrained will of rulers.

questions.q: Name any four of Henkin's eight elements.

questions.q: Which element is directly about protecting citizens' freedoms?

questions.q: Explain how constitutionalism differs from mere possession of a constitution.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?

o: Wheare - government by rule, not arbitrary; Ybema - rulers subject to rules

questions.q: Compare Friedrich's and Wheare's ideas.
questions.a: Friedrich stresses effective restraints and responsibility of government, and Wheare stresses government by rule as opposed to arbitrary rule, limited by the constitution and not just by rulers' desires.

questions.q: Why are independent judiciary and separation of powers both needed for limited government?
questions.a: Separation divides functions so no organ dominates, and an independent judiciary can enforce the limits, checking abuse by other organs.
